# TCP vs UDP: Main Differences

## Connection
- **TCP**: Connection-oriented — requires a handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before data transfer
- **UDP**: Connectionless — just sends packets without establishing a connection

## Reliability
- **TCP**: Guarantees delivery; lost packets are retransmitted
- **UDP**: No delivery guarantee; packets may be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order

## Ordering
- **TCP**: Data arrives in the order it was sent
- **UDP**: No ordering — packets may arrive in any order

## Speed & Overhead
- **TCP**: Slower due to handshakes, acknowledgments, and error checking; header is ~20 bytes
- **UDP**: Faster and lightweight; header is only 8 bytes

## Flow & Congestion Control
- **TCP**: Has flow control (windowing) and congestion control to avoid overwhelming the network
- **UDP**: None — sends at whatever rate the application chooses

## Data Model
- **TCP**: Stream-based — a continuous flow of bytes
- **UDP**: Message-based — discrete datagrams with clear boundaries

## Typical Use Cases

| TCP | UDP |
|-----|-----|
| Web browsing (HTTP/HTTPS) | Video/audio streaming |
| Email (SMTP) | Online gaming |
| File transfer (FTP) | VoIP |
| SSH | DNS lookups |
| | DHCP |

## Rule of Thumb
- Use **TCP** when accuracy and completeness matter more than speed
- Use **UDP** when speed and low latency matter more than perfect delivery (or when the app handles retransmission itself, like QUIC does)
